base_prompt:
January 1, 2026 — A World on Edge
The year 2026 begins without a single conflict defining the international system. Instead, the world is divided by dozens of overlapping crises, rivalries, territorial disputes, economic pressures, proxy wars, and unresolved political conflicts. The Cold War has been over for more than three decades, yet the period of relative optimism that followed its end now feels increasingly distant.
The global economy has survived the shocks of the COVID-19 pandemic, but the recovery has been uneven. Years of disrupted supply chains, energy shocks, high government debt, inflation, demographic pressures, and widening inequality have left many societies vulnerable. Developing countries in particular continue to struggle with debt, food insecurity, weak institutions, and dependence on volatile commodity markets. Global economic growth remains positive, but considerably weaker than the world had hoped, while geopolitical uncertainty continues to weigh on trade and investment.
The international order itself is becoming increasingly fragmented. The United Nations remains the world's principal diplomatic institution, but its ability to resolve major conflicts is increasingly questioned. The great powers frequently disagree within the Security Council, while regional organizations and informal alliances are becoming more important. Major states increasingly pursue their own interests rather than relying on a single international system.
In Europe, the Russia–Ukraine War remains the continent's defining security crisis. Years of fighting have exhausted both sides without producing a decisive settlement. Ukraine continues to depend heavily on Western military and financial support, while Russia has adapted its economy and military production to a prolonged war. Attacks increasingly reach beyond the traditional front lines, while sabotage, cyberattacks, disinformation, and other forms of hybrid warfare have made the boundary between war and peace increasingly difficult to define. The possibility of the conflict spilling beyond Ukraine remains one of Europe's greatest fears.
NATO remains powerful, but its members disagree over how far they should go in confronting Moscow. Eastern European governments demand stronger deterrence, while some Western governments fear that direct confrontation could transform the Ukrainian war into a much larger conflict. Every Russian military move along NATO's borders is therefore watched with extreme caution.
Further south, the Middle East remains deeply unstable. The Israeli-Palestinian conflict continues to generate violence and humanitarian suffering, while armed groups and rival governments compete for influence across the region. Iran's rivalry with Israel and the United States remains particularly dangerous. Lebanon, Syria, Iraq and Yemen remain vulnerable to the actions of competing militias, governments and foreign powers.
In Yemen, the fragile reduction in fighting has never produced a genuine political settlement. The Houthis, internationally recognized authorities, southern separatists and other armed factions continue to compete for territory and influence. Control of the Red Sea and approaches to the Gulf of Aden gives the conflict consequences far beyond Yemen itself. Any major escalation could threaten one of the world's most important maritime trade routes.
The Persian Gulf is similarly tense. Iran's regional influence, Saudi Arabia's ambitions, the security concerns of the Gulf monarchies, and the continuing presence of the United States create a delicate balance. The Strait of Hormuz remains one of the world's most strategically important waterways, meaning that even a localized confrontation could have consequences for energy prices and economies around the globe.
Across Africa, instability takes many different forms. Sudan's civil war has created one of the world's largest humanitarian disasters, while neighboring countries struggle with refugees, weapons trafficking and the possibility of the conflict spreading across borders. The Horn of Africa remains vulnerable to political instability, insurgencies and competition over resources.
Central Africa faces its own collection of crises. Armed groups, weak institutions, ethnic tensions and competition over valuable resources continue to destabilize parts of the region. Relations between the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Rwanda remain particularly dangerous, while neighboring states fear that another major regional war could emerge from local conflicts.
In Myanmar, the military government continues to fight a collection of ethnic armed organizations and opposition forces. Large parts of the country remain outside effective government control, creating a fragmented conflict in which front lines can change rapidly. The longer the war continues, the more difficult a negotiated settlement becomes.
In South Asia, India and Pakistan remain locked in a dangerous rivalry. Their disputes over Kashmir, competing national interests and military postures are made considerably more dangerous by the fact that both possess nuclear weapons. Neither government wants a full-scale war, but history has repeatedly demonstrated how quickly border incidents and political crises can escalate.
India also faces a complicated strategic environment to its east and north. China's growing military and economic power has transformed the balance of power across Asia, while disputes along the Himalayan frontier remain unresolved. Beijing's relations with Taiwan, Japan, India, the Philippines and other regional powers are increasingly intertwined.
In the Taiwan Strait, China continues to regard Taiwan as part of its territory, while Taiwan maintains its de facto self-government. The United States continues to provide Taiwan with political and military support, creating a dangerous strategic triangle. A crisis in the Taiwan Strait would not necessarily begin as a world war—but the possibility that the United States, China and regional allies could become directly involved makes it one of the most consequential potential conflicts on Earth.
Japan is increasingly concerned about its surrounding waters. Chinese military activity around Taiwan and the East China Sea has intensified strategic competition, while the disputed Senkaku/Diaoyu Islands remain a potential flashpoint. Japan's security relationship with the United States means that even a relatively small maritime confrontation could have consequences far beyond the islands themselves.
On the Korean Peninsula, North and South Korea remain technically at war. Pyongyang's nuclear weapons program and missile capabilities continue to worry Seoul, Tokyo and Washington. Any military confrontation could escalate rapidly because of the density of military forces surrounding the peninsula.
Elsewhere in Asia, territorial disputes in the South China Sea continue to pit China against several neighboring states. Maritime patrols, fishing disputes, military construction and competing territorial claims create the possibility of an accidental confrontation. No major power wants a war—but several governments are simultaneously preparing for one.
The Caucasus remains another fragile region. Armenia and Azerbaijan have moved through periods of negotiation and confrontation, but territorial disputes, unresolved grievances and competing regional interests continue to create opportunities for renewed violence. Turkey, Russia and Iran all have significant interests in the region, meaning that a local conflict could quickly acquire an international dimension.
Latin America is comparatively less dominated by interstate warfare, but it is hardly peaceful. Political polarization, organized crime, economic inequality, weak institutions and migration crises continue to destabilize several countries. Mexico struggles with powerful criminal organizations, while Venezuela remains politically and economically troubled. Colombia continues to confront armed groups and criminal organizations despite years of peace efforts.
In the Caribbean and Central America, governments face pressure from organized crime, migration, economic instability and political unrest. These crises rarely threaten to produce a global war, but they can destabilize entire regions and create new humanitarian emergencies.
The world's democracies are also experiencing internal strain. Political polarization has intensified across many major countries. Trust in governments, traditional media and international institutions has declined, while social media allows political movements and disinformation to spread faster than governments can respond. Elections increasingly become moments of international concern rather than purely domestic affairs.
Authoritarian governments, meanwhile, have become increasingly willing to challenge established international norms. Some states rely on military power, others on economic pressure, cyber operations, political interference or proxy forces. The distinction between conventional warfare and hybrid warfare is becoming increasingly blurred.
Technology is accelerating this transformation.
Artificial intelligence, drones, cyberwarfare, satellite surveillance and increasingly sophisticated missile systems are changing how countries prepare for conflict. Governments can now influence events thousands of kilometers away without formally declaring war. A cyberattack against a power grid, a drone strike against a military base, or a blockade of a critical shipping route could create an international crisis before diplomats even understand what happened.
At the same time, the world's dependence on interconnected supply chains has created new vulnerabilities. A war in one region can raise food and fuel prices on another continent. A blockade of a shipping lane can disrupt factories thousands of kilometers away. A financial crisis in one major economy can quickly spread through international markets.
Climate change adds another layer of pressure. Droughts, extreme heat, water shortages, crop failures and increasingly destructive natural disasters place additional stress on governments already struggling with poverty and political instability. Competition over water, food and habitable land is unlikely to create wars by itself, but it can make existing conflicts considerably harder to resolve.
Despite all of this, the world is not yet at war.
Most governments still understand the enormous cost of a major international conflict. Nuclear deterrence remains a powerful barrier against direct confrontation between the great powers. Global trade gives countries strong incentives to avoid destroying the international economy. Diplomats continue to negotiate, ceasefires continue to be attempted, and governments continue to cooperate even while preparing for confrontation.
The problem is that the system is becoming increasingly dependent on restraint.
One border incident could trigger retaliation.
One missile could hit the wrong target.
One political leader could miscalculate.
One collapsing government could create a power vacuum.
One alliance could interpret an attack differently than its opponent intended.
And one regional conflict could pull in a great power that originally had no intention of fighting.
The world therefore enters 2026 in an uneasy state of armed peace. No single crisis is guaranteed to become a global conflict, but the number of possible flashpoints has grown dramatically.
The great powers are watching one another.
Regional powers are building alliances.
Smaller nations are choosing sides—or attempting desperately to remain neutral.
Governments are increasing military spending while publicly calling for peace.
Diplomats are searching for compromises while generals prepare contingency plans.
The international system has not collapsed.
But it is under enormous pressure.
January 1, 2026.
The world has one year ahead of it.
Whether that year brings diplomacy, reform and a gradual return to stability—or whether a series of seemingly unrelated crises combine into something far larger—remains unknown.
The Cold War is over. The age of global confrontation may not be.
Is a global conflict still avoidable?
